title: A Common-Sense Guide to Data Structures and Algorithms
author: Jay Wengrow
summary: The full DSA toolkit for working engineers — from Big O and hash tables to dynamic programming and system design patterns — explained with clarity, practical Python examples, and the mental models that make interview prep and daily work easier.

inspiredBy.title: A Common-Sense Guide to Data Structures and Algorithms in Python
inspiredBy.author: Jay Wengrow

chapters.title: Why Data Structures and Algorithms Matter
chapters.summary: Big O notation is the language of algorithmic efficiency — understanding time and space complexity lets you predict how code scales from 100 rows to 100 million, and knowing when O(n) beats O(log n) in practice is what separates theory from production.

chapters.title: Arrays and Lists in Python
chapters.summary: Python's list is a dynamic array with O(1) amortized append and O(1) index access — but insert and delete are O(n), and knowing when to reach for deque or when list is good enough is daily production reasoning.

chapters.title: Hash Tables (Python dict)
chapters.summary: The hash table is O(1) lookup made real — Python's dict is ordered as of 3.7, uses open addressing with SIMD probing in 3.11+, and understanding collision resolution and load factors explains why dict is almost always the right choice for key-value data.

chapters.title: Stacks and Queues
chapters.summary: Stacks are LIFO, queues are FIFO — use list for stack, collections.deque for queue, and knowing when each data structure fits (DFS uses a stack, BFS uses a queue, undo/redo uses a stack) is pattern recognition that shows up everywhere.

chapters.title: Recursion and the Call Stack
chapters.summary: Recursion is iteration written upside-down — the call stack handles state implicitly, base cases prevent infinite loops, and recognizing when a problem decomposes recursively (trees, divide-and-conquer, backtracking) makes complex algorithms readable.

chapters.title: Sorting Algorithms
chapters.summary: Bubble sort is O(n²) and pedagogical, merge sort is O(n log n) and stable, quicksort is O(n log n) average with O(n²) worst-case, and Python's Timsort combines merge sort and insertion sort to be fast on real-world data with runs and galloping.

chapters.title: Searching: Linear, Binary, and Patterns
chapters.summary: Linear search is O(n), binary search is O(log n) on sorted data, two pointers solve subarray problems in O(n), and sliding window turns nested loops into single passes — these patterns show up in 30% of interview questions and daily data munging.

chapters.title: Trees: Binary, BST, Balanced
chapters.summary: Trees are recursion made visible — binary trees have left and right children, BSTs keep values ordered for O(log n) lookup, AVL and Red-Black trees self-balance to guarantee worst-case bounds, and traversals (in-order, pre-order, post-order, level-order) are the patterns that unlock every tree problem.

chapters.title: Heaps and Priority Queues
chapters.summary: A heap is a binary tree that keeps the min (or max) at the root — Python's heapq gives O(log n) insert and O(log n) extract-min, and priority queues built on heaps power Dijkstra's algorithm, job schedulers, and the top-K pattern that appears constantly.

chapters.title: Graphs: Representation and Traversal
chapters.summary: Graphs are nodes and edges — adjacency lists are space-efficient for sparse graphs, adjacency matrices enable O(1) edge lookup, BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, DFS explores deeply and detects cycles, and recognizing when a problem is secretly a graph (dependencies, state machines, networks) is the DSA superpower.

chapters.title: Dynamic Programming
chapters.summary: Dynamic programming is recursion plus memoization — identify overlapping subproblems, cache results to turn exponential time into polynomial, and the patterns (0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, coin change) repeat across hundreds of interview and real-world optimization problems.

chapters.title: Greedy Algorithms and Advanced Patterns
chapters.summary: Greedy algorithms make the locally optimal choice at each step — they're faster than DP when they work (interval scheduling, Huffman coding, Dijkstra), but proving correctness requires the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure, and backtracking is the escape hatch when greedy fails.

chapters.title: System Design with DSA
chapters.summary: Real systems are DSA composed — an LRU cache is a hash table plus a doubly-linked list, a rate limiter is a sliding window over timestamps, a consistent-hash ring is modular arithmetic plus a balanced tree, and recognizing these building blocks in production architecture questions is what closes the interview loop.
